A Competitor to OpenClaw Emerges
items.content_text: After the success of OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent software that took the tech world by storm earlier this year, it's no surprise that copycats are popping up. And some of these copycats are catching up to OpenClaw, by some measures. Hermes, an agent tool from Nous Research, recently eclipsed OpenClaw in terms of new GitHub contributors in the last 30 days, according to GitHub data compiled by ClawCharts, which tracks the growth of open-source AI agents. (New GitHub contributors are a measure of how strong developer engagement is). And if OpenClaw continues to struggle with evolving from an experimental hacker project to a reliable piece of software, as we've written about here, Hermes and other alternatives like Nvidia's NemoClaw or Genspark Claw would have a bigger opening to break through. Hermes, like OpenClaw, is AI agent software that runs locally on users' devices. It can be used to automate any task you might complete on your computer, like writing code, searching the web for a rare vintage item or sending emails or WhatsApp messages. Nous Research says that what makes Hermes different from OpenClaw is that the agent can teach itself over time how to do the tasks its user asks it to do most often. Hermes does this by automatically writing "skills," or a manual of sorts that tells an agent how to do a task. It writes up these instructions automatically when, for instance, it completes a complex task that requires more than five "tool calls" (such as searching the web or accessing apps like Gmail or Discord) or when it finds a working solution after hitting a bunch of dead ends. (Nous has raised $70 million since its founding in 2023 from investors including Paradigm, OSS Capital and Distributed Global).

items.title: The Information Hires Reporters to Expand Coverage of Nvidia, Musk, Finance, Washington
items.content_text: The Information is pleased to announce four new hires to continue our newsroom's award-winning reporting. They will focus on Nvidia, finance, Elon Musk's companies and tech policy. Dakin Campbell, Finance Dakin brings deep knowledge and a wealth of sources in finance. He has already started to help break news for The Information, reporting on investment banks' trading strategies and the inner workings of complicated AI financing deals. He joins us from Business Insider, where he was chief correspondent for investigations and enterprise, and before that was its chief finance correspondent. He wrote about Oracle's borrowing binge, the true cost of data centers and how big investors, not just individuals, are pulling out of private credit. He was also one of two lead reporters for BI's award-winning project on data centers. Dakin spent eight years at BI and 10 years at Bloomberg, where among many other things, he expanded its San Francisco finance beat following the financial crisis. And he literally wrote the book on tech IPOs: Going Public: How Silicon Valley Rebels Loosened Wall Street's Grip on the IPO and Sparked a Revolution, which featured the memorable IPO valuation metric of "a little crystal-ball gazing and fairy dust." Dakin will be based in New York starting in September. Grace Kay, SpaceX and Tesla Grace has joined The Information to cover SpaceX, Tesla and other Musk companies, where she has already started to break news on xAI. She comes from Business Insider, where she worked for more than five years. There, she covered Tesla, Elon Musk and the broader EV industry. Most recently, Grace worked on BI's enterprise desk, reporting on everything from Tesla's workplace culture and executive turnover to Optimus and the Robotaxi rollout. Over the past year, she's focused on xAI's growing pains and the overlap between Musk's companies. Before BI, she reported on metals and mining at Bloomberg and covered education at Forbes. She is based in New York. Phoebe Liu, Nvidia Phoebe has joined The Information to lead our coverage of Nvidia. Phoebe will get inside the world's most valuable company, which is at the center of a once-in-a-generation boom and led by a relentless CEO doing everything he can to extend its dominance. She's recently gone deep into how Nvidia appears to be winning market share supplying chips for inference. Phoebe is well positioned for this monumental beat, given her work at Forbes over the last three and a half years. She covered numerous billionaire entrepreneurs, wild and shady startups, and scooped an xAI funding pitch. She also took a particular interest in Nvidia co-founder Curtis Priem; CoreWeave, an Nvidia vassal in the neocloud field; and Groq, which Nvidia essentially acquired for $20 billion. She is based in San Francisco. Leo Schwartz, Tech and Politics Leo Schwartz has joined The Information to cover the intersection of politics and tech. He's already started to make an impact, helping break news on Amazon's concerns over the new Anthropic model, the executive AI order and Binance. Leo joined from Fortune magazine, where he has been a senior writer for the last several years covering fintech, crypto, venture capital and financial regulation. At Fortune, he has frequently written about important political figures involved in overseeing tech (from former SEC chair Gary Gensler to Trump advisor Bo Hines). He has chronicled the growing concerns over the Trump business empire's conflicts of interest, broken regulatory news about Elon Musk and tracked the DOGE takeover of the CFPB. He is based in New York.

items.title: Temasek's $75 Billion AI Bet
items.content_text: The prescient investor who appears to hold a crystal ball or have a healthy stomach for risk is always a compelling character to write about. These are the Josh Kushners, Peter Thiels and Masayoshi Sons of the world. Love 'em or hate 'em, they're interesting. At this point of the AI cycle, though, the more important investors to watch might be the ones that evoke little emotion and attract few headlines. They're typically the investors with a more sober approach that has often left them on the sidelines of tech megatrends in the early years. But now they're the new, incremental buyers of AI startup rounds, data center debt and tech stocks, and their patience will be tested if the investment case starts to dampen. That's why I wanted to talk to the investment leaders at Temasek-a low-profile firm that manages hundreds of billions of dollars, with the Singapore government as its sole shareholder, and that is looking to eke out stable returns without lighting cash on fire. It pairs investments in late-stage private tech bets like Stripe and Databricks with older-guard Singapore-based companies it owns huge stakes in, such as Singtel and Singapore Airlines. It holds itself up as a beacon of patient, long-term capital, and it devoted a much larger chunk of its publicly available annual report last year to risk management than it did to AI. Still, the firm has become a silent, deep-pocketed presence in Silicon Valley over the years. And this year, I've noticed its name popping up more often as a new investor in major AI-related megarounds from Anthropic, Isomorphic Labs and Waymo. Temasek is open for business in AI investments, according to Aftab Mathur, the company's managing director, who leads venture and growth investments. He was speaking to me from a glass-walled conference room with a view of Salesforce Tower in downtown San Francisco. The firm planned to triple its investment holdings in AI from $25 billion today to $75 billion by 2030. That would represent about 15% of its projected portfolio overall, up from 7% today, and nearly a quarter of its portfolio outside Singapore, he added. "That's a fairly large jump for Temasek," said Mathur, who is based in Singapore. "We're in a large scale-up in terms of AI exposure." In part what's driving the increased investment interest is what San Francisco-based Temasek Managing Director Martin Fichtner called its "virtuous circle." The firm has watched its large Singapore-based portfolio companies, like $140 billion bank DBS, adopt AI and reduce manual labor, reinforcing investors' views of the technology's value, Fichtner said. The circle is a familiar one to anyone tracking the investment cycle: Corporate adoption of AI drives revenue for AI model and application companies, which supports more capital expenditures for infrastructure, which drives more model investment. Temasek is one face of this. The same patient money is showing up as the private credit financing data centers and the Gulf funds anchoring the megarounds. That's why the tone around AI investing has shifted around the world from cautious to can't miss. Despite the thematic bullishness about the technology overall, important parts of the AI trade still have a hazy outlook. For instance, there are limits to Temasek's bullishness when I asked about the debate of the moment-whether all that AI spending is paying off inside companies. "Whether it's a virtuous circle or not is defined by: Is there an ROI [return on investment]?" Fichtner said. I was also struck by how little Temasek's AI enthusiasts wanted to go out on a limb about where the technology goes from here. Where is AI not working well inside companies? I asked. "It's too early to say," Mathur said. "I think all this is moving so quickly that we're watching, we're tracking....It'd be too early to give an answer one way or another." I asked Mathur and Fichtner which lesser-known AI company might become a household name that embodies its new strategy. Fichtner smiled and gave me a nonanswer. "I'm smiling because I think that's a question that everyone will always want to answer in the rear view mirror, but we will seek diversification," he said. "We think in portfolio terms." That portfolio, of course, is increasingly going to be AI focused. On that big-picture theme, investors are certain. But where exactly will the value lie? And what's still going to blow up? That's where many big-money AI bulls are hedging their answers. items.title: Amazon's Lower Cost AI Chip Offerings Hold Appeal for Businesses
items.content_text: For companies debating which AI server chips to use in their data centers, Amazon appears to have one advantage over Nvidia: price. The cost of using Amazon's Inferentia2 and Trainium's second generation chips to run existing AI models, known as inference, can be 80% lower than Nvidia's H100 chips, for comparable workloads, according to Karol Piatek, who advises companies on their AI infrastructure at Ireland-based consultancy Co Driver Labs. A growing number of businesses that run their own data centers are looking for cheaper and more readily available alternatives to Nvidia chips. Amazon in recent months has discussed using its custom AI chips, Trainium (for developing new models) and Inferentia, with such customers-and the idea is gaining converts.

items.title: AI's New Risk: Unpredictable Government Policies
items.content_text: Investing in AI really is not for the faint of heart. Leaving aside all the worries about risks of huge investments in data centers and the uncertainties about demand, there's also the unpredictable government moves that can upend things. Case in point: the Trump administration's warnings to Anthropic over the weekend that no foreigners, including foreign employees of Anthropic, could access its latest AI models without permission. While that warning is aimed specifically at Anthropic-now in a standoff with the government over its latest AI models-other AI firms are worried about the precedent it sets. As we scooped today, OpenAI executives wrote to staff on Saturday that it had told the administration building AI "requires the best talent from around the world." (See our latest OpenAI scoop, on its first quarter financials, here).

items.title: OpenAI Burned $3.7 Billion in First Three Months of 2026
items.content_text: OpenAI burned through $3.7 billion in the first quarter, more than half its $5.7 billion in revenue, according to documents the company shared with shareholders. Both cash burn and revenue tripled from the same period the previous year, signaling how even with strong AI demand, making money from AI continues to be challenging. The company ended the quarter with more than $73 billion in cash and marketable securities, compared with $40 billion at the end of December, reflecting the company's massive funding round announced at the end of March. Assuming the cash burn remains around the first quarter level, OpenAI won't need to raise more money in the near term. That could relieve the pressure on OpenAI to go public sooner rather than later.
